newsitem.title: CHINA: China police urge unruly villagers to surrender.
newsitem.headline: China police urge unruly villagers to surrender.

text.p: Chinese police have called for the surrender of ringleaders in villages where anger over local elections erupted into violence in southern Guangdong province, local officials said on Monday.
"So far we have made no arrests," said one official of the public security bureau in the mountain town of Wuyun, about 325 km (195 miles) east of the Guangdong provincial capital of Guangzhou.
"However, we have called on those involved in the violence to turn themselves in," he said.
Provincial authorities sent several hundred paramilitary People's Armed Police at the weekend to restore order in the rugged district after a dispute over local elections turned violent.
"There was so much confusion during the clashes that we were unable to identify those involved," the public security official said. "So we hope those responsible will come forward."

Officials said last week's protests were a result of a string of disputes that had built up over several years, including rows over land and the recent failure of local authorities to announce village election results.
The unrest erupted when authorities sent work teams to Wuyun last week to take over management of the village from the local government, officials said.
The work teams fanned out into about five smaller mountain villages around Wuyun, an area with a population of about 30,000, and several were attacked and beaten up, they said.
No one was seriously injured, they said.

Villagers were angered by the failure of the Wuyun government to announce the results of local village elections, and some angry supporters of ousted local government officials attacked the working group sent in from outside, they said.
China has introduced a system of grassroots village elections by which farmers can elect their local government representatives in multi-candidate polls.

While in many areas villagers elect existing local leaders, seeing them as representing stability, the system has also raised the possibility that local vested interests who lose the confidence of their electorate can lose their positions.
The area was now calm, officials said.
